title: Sony QSSR Upscaler Expands to Spider-Man 2, ARC Raiders, No Man’s Sky & More【TechPowerUp】
body:
Sony has broadened the reach of its Quick Super Sampling Rendering (QSSR) technology, bringing the AI‑driven upscaler to six additional PlayStation 5 titles, including the highly anticipated Marvel’s Spider‑Man 2. The update, which went live this week, adds QSSR support to both the Fidelity and Performance modes of the new blockbuster, while other games such as ARC Raiders, No Man’s Sky, Control Resonance, and two yet‑to‑be‑named releases will receive the enhancement over the coming months. The move marks another step in Sony’s effort to narrow the visual gap between the base PS5 and its more powerful “Pro” variant without requiring new hardware.

QSSR, first introduced as a lightweight alternative to the more resource‑intensive FidelityFX Super Resolution (FSR) and Nvidia’s DLSS, works by applying a trained neural network to upscale lower‑resolution frames in real time. The result is a smoother frame rate and sharper image quality that can be toggled on the fly, allowing developers to retain high‑fidelity visuals while meeting the 60 fps target that many modern titles aim for. For PS5 owners who do not own the forthcoming PS5 Pro, the rollout represents a tangible boost in visual performance, especially on games that previously forced a trade‑off between resolution and speed.

Marvel’s Spider‑Man 2, developed by Insomniac Games, is the first title to receive the QSSR patch. Players can now enable the upscaler in the game’s settings, choosing between the “Fidelity” mode, which prioritises 4K resolution, and the “Performance” mode, which targets 60 fps. Early benchmarks suggest that QSSR narrows the gap between the two modes, delivering near‑4K clarity in the performance setting with only a modest increase in GPU load. Insomniac’s lead technical director, Bryan Dinh, explained that the integration required minimal code changes because QSSR is built into the PS5’s operating system, allowing the studio to focus on fine‑tuning the neural network’s parameters rather than re‑architecting the rendering pipeline.

The upcoming wave of QSSR‑enabled games underscores Sony’s broader strategy to extend the lifespan of the current console generation. ARC Raiders, a fast‑paced battle‑royale shooter, will benefit from QSSR’s ability to keep frame rates stable during large‑scale engagements, while No Man’s Sky’s procedurally generated planets will appear sharper without sacrificing the fluidity needed for exploration. Control Resonance, the latest entry in Remedy’s critically acclaimed franchise, is set to receive the upscaler in a December patch, promising a more immersive experience in its hyper‑realistic environments. By delivering these updates through standard firmware patches, Sony avoids the need for developers to ship separate “Pro‑only” versions, simplifying the ecosystem for both creators and consumers.

Industry analysts view the expansion as a pragmatic response to the mixed reception of the PS5 Pro, which many felt offered only incremental improvements over the base console. “Sony is essentially democratizing the benefits of higher‑end hardware through software,” noted Maya Patel, senior analyst at DigiTrend. “If QSSR can consistently deliver a perceptible boost across a diverse library, it could set a new standard for how console manufacturers address hardware limitations without forcing users into costly upgrades.” The approach also mirrors trends in the PC space, where AI‑based upscaling has become commonplace, but its adoption on consoles has been slower due to stricter certification processes and hardware constraints.

Looking ahead, Sony has hinted that additional titles will join the QSSR roster throughout 2025, and the company is already exploring next‑generation iterations of the technology that could leverage the PS5 Pro’s upgraded GPU cores for even higher quality upscaling. For now, base‑model PS5 owners can expect a noticeable visual uplift in some of the year’s most talked‑about releases, reinforcing Sony’s commitment to extending the console’s relevance in a rapidly evolving gaming landscape. As more developers embrace QSSR, the line between “standard” and “enhanced” hardware experiences may continue to blur, offering gamers richer visuals without the need for new consoles.
